paper_a.title: Incentives in Web Studies: Methodological Issues and a Review

paper_b.title: Response Rates of Online Surveys in Published Research: A Meta-Analysis
paper_b.authors: Meng-Jia Wu, Kelly Zhao, Francisca Fils-Aime

conflicting_claim: Offering material incentives significantly increases response rates in online surveys.
evidence_a: Results section: Across 32 web survey experiments with over 212,000 participants, offering material incentives significantly increases the odds of starting a web survey (OR = 1.19, p < .001) as well as finishing it (OR = 1.27).
evidence_b: Abstract & Results section (Section 3): Across 1,071 online survey response rates from published education research, using incentives shows no statistically significant effect on overall response rates compared to factors like pre-contacting participants or sending reminders.
explanation: Göritz finds in a meta-analysis of controlled experiments that material incentives reliably boost participation and completion in web surveys. In contrast, Wu et al. analyze over a thousand published online surveys and find that incentives make no significant difference to response rates, likely because observational comparisons across diverse studies mask within-experiment incentive effects.
